name: Coushatta
packetScope: Bounded Texas-priority Coushatta review. Six substantive distinct works, one short inspected supporting language page and one retained original archive route whose content was unavailable. All three original IDs/URLs preserved; no Site edits, contacts, delegation or source-media use.
proposedOverview: Coushatta, also called Koasati, histories connect Louisiana, Texas and Oklahoma communities. This guide distinguishes particular governments, historical movement, shared institutions and community-directed language work.
relationshipNote: Coushatta/Koasati people are not interchangeable with Alabama people. The Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana, Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas and Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town in Oklahoma are distinct governments and communities. Their connections do not make every family’s route, language use or political history identical. A joint government is not evidence of a single original people.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: The shared Texas government has a particular history
claimBlocks.text: The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas describes Alabama and Coushatta as separate peoples with a long association. Its history connects migration into East Texas with relationships under successive colonial and state governments. The Tribe’s timeline dates federal restoration to 1987. This public account concerns the joint Texas institution, rather than making Louisiana and Oklahoma Coushatta communities branches of that government.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Village leaders and a changing institutional name
claimBlocks.text: The Tribe’s Chief History distinguishes leaders of Alabama villages, leaders of Coushatta villages and later Alabama-Coushatta chiefs. It names Coushatta leaders associated with different Texas communities and describes movement onto the Alabama reservation beginning in 1859. The publication’s structure makes village-level histories visible; it should not be read as proof that every earlier Coushatta community belonged to one unchanged modern government.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Attributed 2014-program introduction; Coushatta chiefs; transition to shared chiefs

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Louisiana’s account of movement and institutional renewal
claimBlocks.text: The Louisiana Tribe’s history describes successive settlements across a changing colonial borderland and an enduring community near Elton. It attributes renewed federal recognition in 1973 to years of community organizing and advocacy after services were withdrawn. These are the Tribe’s institutional historical statements. Its trajectory differs from the Texas restoration chronology and does not establish current eligibility, services or every family’s migration.

Bertney and Linda Langley describe a Koasati Language Committee whose members made spelling decisions and shaped practical teaching materials. Their account connects workshops, documentation training and collaborative review with community control of the resulting work. It records activities beginning in 2006–2007, rather than current program delivery. The chapter explains a process; its reported successes are not an independently measured learner-fluency outcome.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Texas connections extend beyond present government locations
claimBlocks.text: TxDOT’s April 2021 report explicitly acknowledges collaboration with the Coushatta Tribe of Louisiana’s heritage staff. It describes several Coushatta communities in Texas and related travel networks connecting Texas and Louisiana. The account treats village decisions and movements separately. This history helps explain why a Louisiana-based government can have Texas interests; it is not a new territorial boundary or a claim that everyone followed one route.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Introduction 3; village/trail discussion 9–12; differing settlement choices 16–17

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: The Oklahoma town’s own historical perspective
claimBlocks.text: Alabama-Quassarte Tribal Town describes Alabama and Quassarte as earlier distinct towns within the Muscogee Confederacy. Its history differentiates people who moved southwest into Louisiana and Texas from those removed with the Creeks to Indian Territory. The Oklahoma community’s continuing institutional story is therefore a separate reading path, rather than another name for the Texas or Louisiana government.

The Louisiana Tribe identifies Koasati as a Muskogean language and connects its community with speakers in Louisiana and Texas. Alabama is listed as a related language, rather than an alternative name for Koasati. This short orientation supplies no present speaker census or universal account of language use across all Coushatta communities.

initialAdequacy.rationale: Six substantial historical/educational works provide distinct Texas, Louisiana and Oklahoma perspectives, including community publications and a community-coauthored language-project account. This supports a bounded cited introduction with explicit gaps. It does not reach the twelve-source target, complete a deep dive, establish current conditions or imply community endorsement.
remainingLimits: Archive access and actual learner-facing grammar/textbook reading remain open.
Independent original legal/archival records and further Coushatta-authored scholarship would deepen the historical claims.
Dated reports and undated institutional narratives do not establish present demographics, leadership, services or language outcomes.
